exercise1.prompt: Grouping by Several Keys: Count every pair

hiddenCases.name: each distinct pair gets its own entry
pairs that never occur are absent

exercise1.hint: Group by both columns and ask for size. to_dict() on a two-level index gives tuple keys, and the counts want int() to shed their numpy type.

exercise2.prompt: Grouping by Several Keys: Flatten it back to a table

hiddenCases.name: the keys are columns, not an index
the summarised column keeps its name
the grouping is done by pandas
hiddenCases.describe: a groupby rather than a hand-written loop

exercise2.hint: Group by the two columns, take the mean of score, then reset_index() to push both levels back out as columns. Without it the keys stay in the index and the columns list is just ["score"].

questions.prompt: What does grouping by two keys give you?
choices: A row per combination, with a two-level index
questions.explain: One group-by, not two, and the index carries both keys.

questions.prompt: How do you turn the two index levels back into columns?
questions.explain: unstack lays the grid out instead, which is a different and also useful shape.

questions.prompt: A subject/year pair has no rows. What appears in the result?
questions.explain: You get one row per combination that occurs, not per combination that is possible. unstack shows the gaps as NaN.

questions.prompt: How do you read one cell out of a two-level result?
choices: Both of the first two work
questions.explain: A tuple indexes both levels at once; naming just the first gives you everything underneath it.
